interviewQuestions.question: Why does Android need a dedicated DI framework like Hilt instead of just using constructor injection everywhere?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Constructor injection assumes you control where an object is created — you write `new Foo(dependency)` somewhere, and that's your injection point. Android breaks that assumption for anything the OS instantiates directly: an Activity or Fragment is created by the framework when a component launches, not by a line of your own code, so there's no constructor call site available to pass dependencies into.

Before something like Hilt existed, the common workaround was a service locator: a global-ish container that an Activity pulls dependencies *from* inside `onCreate`. That works, but it reverses the direction DI is meant to have — a class reaching out to grab what it needs, rather than declaring its needs and having them supplied — which makes dependencies harder to see at a glance and harder to swap for fakes in a test, since the pull-based lookup is baked into the class rather than expressed as parameters.

Hilt closes this by generating the plumbing needed to still get constructor-style, declared-and-supplied injection into framework-instantiated classes, via annotations processed at compile time. It also maps its dependency-scoping hierarchy directly onto Android's own lifecycle containment (Application → Activity → Fragment/ViewModel), so a dependency's lifetime can be tied cleanly to the Android lifecycle it should actually match, which a hand-rolled service locator would have to reimplement itself.

**Testing:** whether you understand the specific structural reason (framework-controlled instantiation) rather than reciting "DI is good practice" without the Android-specific motivation.

interviewQuestions.question: A build fails with a Hilt error about a dependency cycle between two of your classes. How would you approach fixing it, beyond just making the compiler happy?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd treat the compile-time failure as useful information rather than an obstacle to route around, because a genuine circular dependency between two classes is almost always a symptom that the responsibilities are split wrong, not a limitation of the DI framework to work around with a trick.

First, I'd look at what each class actually needs from the other. If class A needs B only to call one or two specific methods, and B needs A the same way, that's usually a sign there's a piece of shared logic or shared state that both are independently reaching for — the fix is extracting that into a third class C that both A and B depend on, which breaks the cycle by removing the reason either needed the other directly in the first place.

If instead the relationship is genuinely event-based — A needs to be notified when something happens in B, and B needs to be notified when something happens in A — I'd replace the direct constructor dependency with a callback or event-listener pattern, so neither class holds a hard reference to the other's fully-constructed instance; they communicate through a registered listener instead, which sidesteps the construction-order problem entirely.

What I'd specifically avoid is reaching for `Lazy<T>` injection or a manual provider function purely to silence the compiler without addressing why the cycle exists — that technically compiles but usually just defers the actual design problem to a runtime null-check or an implicit ordering assumption that's much harder to reason about than the compile-time error was.

**Testing:** whether you treat a DI cycle error as a design signal to investigate, rather than a technical obstacle to route around with the first workaround that compiles.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you decide the correct Hilt scope for a new dependency — say, a cache of the user's currently selected filters on a search screen?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start from what the dependency actually represents and how long that thing should logically live, not from convenience or from copying whatever scope a similar-looking class already uses elsewhere in the codebase.

A cache of the user's currently selected filters is specific to one screen's session — it shouldn't survive navigating away and back (that would be a stale-state bug, showing old filters on a fresh visit) and it doesn't need to be shared across the whole app the way a network client does. That points toward `@ViewModelScoped` if it's naturally owned alongside a ViewModel's other state (surviving rotation, dying when the screen genuinely goes away) or `@ActivityScoped` if it's more tightly coupled to the View layer itself and doesn't need to survive rotation independently.

What I'd explicitly rule out: `@Singleton`. It would work mechanically — the code would compile and run — but it's the wrong lifetime for state that's conceptually tied to one screen visit; a `@Singleton`-scoped filter cache would persist stale filters into a later, unrelated visit to the same screen, or leak Activity-specific selection state well past when it should have been cleared.

The test I apply generally: does this dependency represent something the whole app shares (network client, database) — `@Singleton`; something scoped to one screen's lifetime including rotation — `@ViewModelScoped`; something tied more tightly to the View itself — `@ActivityScoped`/`@FragmentScoped`. Getting this right up front avoids both the resource waste of over-scoping and the stale-state or leak risk of under-scoping.

**Testing:** whether you can reason from the dependency's actual semantics to the correct scope, rather than defaulting to whatever scope is already used elsewhere in the codebase.

interviewQuestions.question: As a staff engineer, what DI-related code smells would prompt you to push back in review, even if the code compiles and passes tests?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Several patterns compile fine, pass tests, and still represent real risk that only shows up later — I'd flag these specifically because Hilt's compile-time checks catch outright scope violations but not the subtler versions.

First: any Application-scoped (`@Singleton`) class that holds a reference — direct or indirect, through a listener or callback — to something Activity-scoped. Hilt's compiler catches the most direct version of this, but a callback registered by an Activity-scoped object and stored in a longer-lived singleton's field can slip through, producing the exact Context-leak pattern from the lifecycle topic, just introduced via DI wiring instead of a hand-written static field.

Second: a proliferation of scopes that don't map to anything meaningful — a dependency marked `@ActivityScoped` purely because that's what was copy-pasted from a nearby class, with no actual reason it needs to be shared within an Activity rather than freshly created each time. This isn't a correctness bug on its own, but it signals the team is applying scoping annotations by pattern-matching rather than reasoning about actual lifetime needs, which tends to produce real bugs eventually as the codebase grows.

Third: modules that provide overly broad or vague types — a `@Provides` function returning a raw `OkHttpClient` with no scope annotation at all, used inconsistently across the codebase, some call sites assuming it's shared and others not. I'd want every provided dependency's intended sharing behavior to be explicit and consistent, not implicit and assumed.

I'd frame all of this to the team not as "Hilt rules" but as the same underlying principle from the Activity lifecycle topic — never let something with a longer lifetime hold a standing reference to something with a shorter one — since DI scoping mistakes and manual Context leaks are the same bug wearing different clothes.

**Testing:** whether you can spot DI-specific versions of a general lifecycle-safety principle, rather than treating DI correctness as a separate, unrelated concern from lifecycle management.
